#9632. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9631. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9630. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9629. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

#9628. A Seven-Slide Framework for Funding AI Transformation Without New Headcount

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

"Go. What will it cost?" That was the CTO's whole answer to the AI transformation pitch. Two days later the roadmap for next year was exactly the same size.

An AI business case, for a VP of Engineering, is a request for roadmap capacity. In the org I'm thinking of, about 100 engineers shrank to roughly 40 or 50 available for next year's roadmap once production care and the AI work were counted honestly. The money question was answered in one sentence. The capacity question nearly killed the plan.

Let's call the VP Tomas. He brought his deck to one of our sessions. The extra hires he'd planned for were gone, so the transformation had to be paid out of the roadmap.

His Head of Product agreed with the numbers on his slides. Their wishlist for next year didn't lose a single theme.

The planning offsite is a few weeks away.

Tomas's capacity slide showed how ~100 engineers shrink to the people left for new work. Engineers read it in five seconds. His Head of Product read it as engineering's problem, not as a list of things to drop.

Incidents, support, upgrades, the work that isn't on any roadmap

What a roadmap silently assumes is the whole team

The people building the AI setup, plus the slowdown in streams while they switch

Ranges from one real engineering org, anonymised. Your numbers will differ, the shape won't.

That table is the business case. The CFO question ("is it worth the money") was cheap, because there was no new money. The real cost is that half of what product thought it could build next year doesn't fit.

If you're still hiring the person who will own this, my Head of AI transformation playbook covers the first six months of that seat. This post is about the sell before it.

The CTO's yes is the cheap yes. The expensive one is your Head of Product's, because they pay for it with their roadmap, and the pressure from above to deliver all of it lands on them first.

So they agree in the meeting and the roadmap doesn't move two days later. That's product denial, and from my experience it's part of the development, part of the battle. It isn't bad faith. It's what a person does when the only thing on the table is a loss.

The standard advice points somewhere else. Oracle's guide to the business case for AI, the top US Google result for "AI transformation business case" on the day I wrote this (12 November 2026), is about justifying AI investments "based on solid ROI calculations", and its first step is an AI center-of-excellence committee. That's the right case for a company buying software.

It wasn't Tomas's problem. The ROI wasn't the question; the CTO had already said go.

The person whose roadmap pays for it hadn't been asked anything.

Without an answer to "what's in it for me", they stay in denial. And from where they sit, that's rational.

When Tomas walked me through his deck, his message was "you need to cut your roadmap". I stopped him there, because I've watched this exact sentence lose the room.

It's not that I want you to cut your roadmap. It's that we cut our roadmap together. The moment you start using "you" instead of "we", you're screwed.

I know it sounds stupid. It helped me enormously for the rest of my career.

I learned it at Mews, while engineering grew from 8 to 80 teams. In one quarterly planning, I told our product lead: "You need to drop two features so we can rebuild the platform. The rest of the hour went into defending both. Next quarter, same numbers on the slide, I asked which two we drop together. We agreed in fifteen minutes. You take the weapon out of the other person's hands, because they no longer feel pushed into a corner.

The slide has to say it too. Tomas had one cut slide with a lot of small numbers about product areas. What I wanted to see is two numbers: product minus x percent, platform minus y percent.

In the example table further down that's product −60% of the wishlist and platform −33%. The platform team sits under the VP of Engineering, so the second number is his own cut, visible, next to theirs. Now you're playing the same game.

Tomas's punchline, the gain, sat on slide 9. By slide 9 the Head of Product has spent eight slides hearing what they're losing. Move it to slide 2.

One line: "We propose to fund the AI transformation from next year's roadmap: product −x%, platform −y%, for a gain we both commit to." The room knows from the first minute what it's being asked to approve.

The payoff first. In Tomas's model a stream that's transforming drops to about 30% of its normal throughput for a few months, then comes back faster, with break-even around mid-year and roughly 3x by the end of the year. It's a model, not a measurement, and slide 7 is where somebody commits to it.

The second card I gave him is a risk, not a gain: if we don't do it, customers churn to competitors who ship the AI features first. Ask your sales or customer-success lead which deals already mention it.

The burndown table above. Colour it: what's under the line red, what's above the line green. Yes, it's basic. You want people to understand it in five seconds.

Product −x%, platform −y%, side by side. Nobody in the room should be able to say "engineering wants us to cut".

Not just that we cut, but how: reduce the scope, stretch the timeline, or drop the item. To go one step further, give an AI model your roadmap list and the capacity table and ask it to propose what to delay or drop. Careful: it's a proposal, not an order.

Cost of delay is "a way of communicating the impact of time on the outcomes we hope to achieve": what does each month without this cost us? Put that number on every item you're stretching.

Then translate it into CFO language: yes, we slow down and it shows in 2027, and here is what 2028 and 2029 look like if the model holds.

The Head of Product commits to the option they picked, because they get the boost out of it. The VP of Engineering commits to the multiplier. Both commitments on the table, in writing. Without them the meeting is an opinion poll.

Here's the table I asked Tomas to rebuild for the offsite, filled in for a made-up company so you can see the shape. Every name and number in it is invented.

Keep, cut scope to the payment-provider switch

The column that does the work is "% of plan". In Tomas's case one area's real capacity came out at roughly a third of what product had assumed, because the earlier estimate missed production care and the AI dip. A percentage per area lets your Head of Product decide what to cut, which is the point.

Download the blank version: the AI business case template (zip, 3 KB) has the capacity table as a CSV for Excel or Google Sheets and the seven-slide outline as Markdown, with one example line per field that you delete.

Ask yourself one question first: how do you want the offsite to end? Go backwards from that.

The VP of Engineering and the Head of Product walk in as one team and say three things. This is the situation. This is our proposal, with one alternative and its impact. These are the initiatives we struck out, please challenge and confirm.

By the end the impact is clear and you have a mandate. Let's be honest, two initiatives will still be argued about.

Amazon replaced slide decks with six-page memos read in silence at the start of the meeting. You don't need to go that far. Send the seven slides plus one page of context two days before.

Put the full capacity table in it, so in the room you can say "don't look at the table now, look at it later if you want". Expect people to throw it into their AI tools to check your math. Good, let them.

The term comes from Henry Kissinger's 1974 rounds between Middle East capitals. Your version is cheaper: before the offsite, walk the proposal past each decision maker one by one and ask what would make them say no. Nothing in the room should be a surprise.

If you need your boss to take pressure off your Head of Product for the next two quarters, ask here, in a one-to-one, not in the meeting. How to influence your manager is the same muscle.

A strong product person removes the items with the lowest value. A weak one makes compromises: we keep everything on the roadmap, because removing it looks bad, and we just stretch it all. Stretching one item with a new date is a decision; stretching everything is avoidance.

RICE, Intercom's reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort score, is enough for this. Score the list and the strikes become obvious.

"If we don't do it, our financial results will hold" is the assumption to break. Your customers will get the AI features somewhere else.

So this isn't about delivering something later. It's about whether the company is still in the race in 2028.

Tomas had the go from the top in one sentence. He's rebuilding the deck around a peer, a table and two percentages, and the offsite is still ahead of him. The method is the bet; the room hasn't voted yet.

Which of your peers owns the roadmap you're paying with?

Price it in roadmap capacity, not in money. Start from total engineering FTE, subtract the people who keep production running, subtract the AI team and the transition dip, and show what is left for next year's roadmap. Then propose where product and platform each cut, with a percentage per side, and put the payoff on the second slide.

Make it a shared cut. Show product minus x percent and platform minus y percent on one slide, answer what product gets back before you show the cost, and offer two or three ways to cut instead of one order. Walk the proposal past each decision maker one by one before the planning meeting, so nothing in the room is a surprise.

Seven: the decision you need, what's in it for product, where the capacity really goes, the shared cut as two percentages, two or three ways to cut, cost of delay against the gain, and what each leader commits to. Send it as a pre-read before the meeting.

Both, together. When the VP of Engineering presents alone, the room hears an engineering ask and product defends its roadmap. When the VP of Engineering and the Head of Product present one proposal and each commits to a number, the room is approving a plan, not refereeing a fight.

#9627. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9626. System One Models and the Future of AI Decision-Making

Models have been superhuman at chat for years, and the industry still can't point to where all the automation went.

Diogo Almeida, who helped build the instruction-following research that became ChatGPT, spent four years on that question before he left OpenAI. His answer, shipped in September 2026 as TypeSafe AI's Jev, is that the bottleneck was never raw intelligence. It's the interface. A model that replies in prose is an awkward component to build software on, because software doesn't consume sentences. It consumes values.

The class TypeSafe calls System One is named after the fast, intuitive thinking in Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. A System One model takes unstructured state in and returns typed probabilistic decisions out, with no chat interface and no string generation. Using a general-purpose generative model in that role wastes tokens and processing time at scale.

Every pipeline I've built has the same point of friction: somewhere a language model writes prose and my code reads it back. The application wants a decision about keeping or deleting an email, or classifying a ticket as escalation. A frontier model generates a full paragraph containing the reasoning and the one-word decision, and the response gets routed through a parser to extract that word.

The waste shows up in four places at once. Output tokens cost three to eight times the input price on most providers, and a classification answer is mostly output. The response is a string, so it has to be parsed, and JSON mode wraps the real answer in a structure that can multiply the token count five to ten times on a small task like email classification. The value then needs validation against a schema, because a generative model can emit a response you never defined. And when any of that fails, retry blocks cost another full generation. A task whose substance is a single yes or no bills like a small essay.

There's a fifth cost that doesn't show on the invoice. A generative model is systematically overconfident. Ask for a confidence score and you get one, but the number isn't calibrated, so you can't branch on it. A model that's right 95% of the time and can't tell you which calls are in the other 5% can't run unattended. You keep a human in the loop because you have no way to know when the model needs one.

The agent loop makes this worse, because an agent makes a decision at every step. Every decision is another model call, and the loop slows down on retries and unverifiable responses.

Jev gives up string generation entirely. You declare the shape of the answer up front and call it like a function: send a state and a set of questions, and get the fields back filled in, each with a calibrated probability attached. TypeSafe describes it as a frontier-intelligence function call.

Parallel sampling. A chat model builds its answer one token at a time, each conditioned on the last. Jev fills every field in a single pass. TypeSafe reports end-to-end response times of 70 to 500 milliseconds against 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models, and you can ask several questions about the same state in one request without meaningfully changing the response time. That's where the 40x to 200x speed claims come from.

Schema conformance by construction. The possible outputs are enumerated before the call, so a wrong model decision cannot produce a type error. TypeSafe's 0% type-error figure is derived from the construction of the responses, not from testing.

Calibrated confidence. Every answer ships with a probability. TypeSafe trains with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) instead of RLHF, so those probability numbers are genuinely accurate: if the confidence is high, the accuracy is high. That predictability is what makes the model composable into systems that run unattended.

The question types map onto what software actually asks. A Noul answers yes or no and returns the probability the statement is true. A Choice picks from a set of up to 255 options and returns a probability per option plus an overall confidence. A Score rates the input against ordered levels like low, medium, high. Keep or drop, route to tier two or tier three, is this urgent. Each question maps to a line of code that returns a typed value.

The pricing is the other half of the story. Jev costs $0.042 per million input tokens, and output is free, because there is no output in the billing sense. TypeSafe advertises it as 238 times cheaper on input than Claude Fable 5.1's $10 per million. A frontier chat model lists around $5 per million input and $25 to $30 per million output, and output is exactly where a classification answer lives.

Small numbers hide the story. Volume exposes it. Here's the cost function:

Run that at a million decisions a day and the difference stops being trivia. The generative model bills about $5,400 for that volume. Jev bills about $25. Third-party measurements land between the extremes: one group measured 1,000 eight-way routing decisions at $0.015 on Jev against $0.61 on GPT-5.6 Terra, about 40x. TypeSafe's own workflow evals claim 444.6x cheaper, and LangChain repeats 400x lower cost on classification tasks. Whatever the honest middle is, it's two orders of magnitude, and it's structural, not a price war.

The gap isn't because Jev is a smaller model that happens to be good enough. It's because a generative model bills you for the process of producing prose, and a decision doesn't need prose. Output tokens, parsing, validation, retries, and the uncertainty tax all disappear together because the model was built not to generate strings in the first place.

The instinct when you see that ratio is to reach for a cheaper generative model instead. That isn't the fix. A smaller generative model still produces a string, still needs parsing and validation, and still reports confidence you can't trust. It lowers the price per call and leaves the structural waste exactly where it was. The waste is in the interface, not the invoice.

Same routing decision, two implementations. First, the generative approach that most early pipelines used:

Now the System One version, using the TypeSafe SDK shape:

The second version has no parse step, no validation step, and no failure path where the model returns a value you didn't allow. The schema was part of the request, so the contract is enforced before the call rather than after it.

The difference that matters most is what happens with an ambiguous ticket. In the first version, confidence is a string the model made up. In the second, it's a number you can trust enough to branch on:

That branch is the whole automation argument in one line. When the model can tell you it's uncertain, you route the uncertain cases to a human and let the confident ones run unattended. The model doesn't need to be right every time. It needs to be honest about when it isn't, and the system around it becomes reliable even though the model isn't.

This isn't hypothetical for me. My own news filter uses a small Jev call to decide keep or drop before spending a full LLM on anything worth reading. A logged run came back at 354 input tokens and a probability, total. The expensive model never sees the boring stuff.

Nothing here argues against generative models. They're for open-ended reasoning and generation, and nothing replaces them there. The argument is about the division of labor inside an LLM operation: the big model thinks and writes, and the decision points around it run on something shaped like a function call.

The early deployments show the pattern. LangChain's Open SWE router originally classified requests with an LLM using structured output, then switched to Jev and made classification almost 50 times faster. In the A/B test that mattered, routing 973 agent threads across model tiers cut the median cost per thread 64%, from $2.61 to $0.94, with no measurable quality change. The same team ran the opposite experiment, routing everything to the cheapest model, and killed it within a day because engineers said output quality was disrupting their work. Cheapness was never the objective. Fitting the tool to the task was.

The guardrail pattern is the one I expect to spread. Coding harnesses like Claude Code and Cursor already classify dangerous actions before taking them, but the classifier lived in their closed-source code. A cheap, calibrated decision model lets any agent apply the same gate before a tool execution by asking Jev whether the call is risky, and blocking it if the answer is yes. LangChain shipped exactly that as Auto Mode middleware over Jev.

None of this requires believing TypeSafe's biggest numbers. The workflow-eval claims of 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper come from the vendor's own evaluations, built by its own team, scored against models the vendor chose. The intelligence-parity claim is only about System One shaped tasks, not general capability.

What you can verify yourself is the price, the latency on your own calls, and the schema guarantee, which is falsifiable by a single bad response. Treat the launch numbers as the ceiling, measure your own workload, and expect the real ratio to land somewhere between 40x and 400x. That's still a big number, and it doesn't depend on marketing.

The name Jev comes from William Stanley Jevons, the economist who noticed that making steam engines more efficient increased the demand for coal rather than reducing it. Cheaper steam meant more uses for steam. TypeSafe's bet is that machine intelligence follows the same path: every order of magnitude drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks orders of magnitude more use cases. Their own Doom demo runs about ten queries a second, which they estimate costs around seven dollars an hour, and their reaction was that this was cheaper than expected. A few years ago that sentence would not have existed.

The price and the interface put decisions inside ordinary code paths for the first time. The chatbot race never did that. When a routing decision costs a fraction of a cent and answers in a hundred milliseconds, you stop treating AI as a service you call for special occasions and start treating it as an if-statement that happens to be learned. Projects involving decision-making at scale, such as the map-reduce over a petabyte of unstructured data, or the email triage that never sleeps, never made sense at frontier prices with prose responses. They make sense at $0.042 per million input tokens with typed outputs.

Software was never waiting for a model that could write better. It was waiting for a model that could decide, cheaply enough and honestly enough to be trusted with the boring work. The big generative models will keep getting better at thinking and writing. The decisions in between will increasingly be made by models that don't write at all.

#9625. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.

The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9624. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9623. Who owns your AI agent when something goes wrong?

When something goes wrong with an AI agent, the first question is simple: who owns it? In many companies the answer is "the team." That sounds like shared responsibility, but in practice it means no single person is watching the agent, and no single person can say "stop."

Disclosure: I run a small AI agent risk-check service called AgentRisk, so this topic is close to my work.

An agent is not a one-time project. Its model gets updated, its prompts get tweaked, its permissions grow, and the people around it change jobs. Each of those changes needs someone who notices and decides what to do.

When ownership is spread across a group, a few things tend to happen:

The fix is small. Give every agent exactly one named human owner. That person does not have to do all the work, but they are the one who:

A shared spreadsheet is enough to start. Columns: agent, purpose, owner, backup, last reviewed.

Ownership has to survive reorganizations. When someone changes roles or leaves, their agents should be reassigned as part of that process, the same way you would reassign their accounts and shared documents. Naming a backup keeps there from ever being a gap.

Make a list of every agent you run, and put a name next to each one. If you can't name a person for one of them, that tells you something useful: it is either unowned and needs an owner, or unused and should be turned off.
