#9598. The Technical Challenges of Moving Tokenized Deposits Between Banks

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

Tech Writer | AI, Cybersecurity & Software Content Specialist

A bank can issue a deposit token on a blockchain and let approved customers transfer it around the clock. But when the recipient uses a different bank, spending that money may require extra steps.

Suppose a company receives $500,000 in tokenized deposits from a trading partner. The tokens arrive in its wallet, and the company wants to use the funds to pay a supplier through its usual bank. If that bank cannot accept the tokens, the company must find another way to access the money, such as redeeming the tokens with the issuing bank and transferring the funds through an existing payment system.

For a business managing money across several banks, that extra step can limit the usefulness of tokenized deposits. The transfer may be quick, but the recipient still needs a practical way to use the funds.

Banks are working on this problem as they bring deposits onto programmable networks. Improving blockchain performance helps, but it does not settle the questions that arise when money moves between institutions.

A tokenized deposit represents a deposit held in a commercial bank. It means that the deposit stays with the bank regardless of where the transactions related to it are executed on the blockchain.

A token issued by Bank A is not necessarily a deposit with Bank B just because it is delivered to Bank B's customer. The recipient bank must understand whether it can accept the token, what rights the holder has and how to process the payment.

Let us go back to the firm that receives the $500,000. Its treasury staff can cash out the tokens from Bank A and transfer the funds through a traditional payment method. Alternatively, the two banks can come to an agreement that would enable them to clear the transaction without requiring the recipient to handle the original tokens.

Both approaches depend on rules that the institutions recognize and are prepared to follow. Bank B needs to know when it can credit the company's account and what to do in case of a failed transfer or cash-out. In his October 2026 speech, Piero Cipollone from the European Central Bank emphasized that one euro issued by a regulated bank should be exchangeable at par with a euro issued by another regulated bank.

For businesses, the concern is practical. Receiving money from a trading partner should not create additional hurdles simply because the payment originated on another bank's blockchain.

Consider a payment where a customer of Bank A makes a transfer of tokenized dollars to a supplier whose account is maintained at Bank B. First off, Bank B must ascertain whether it is willing to accept the payment. The process requires identification of the issuing bank, and also checking that the token and the transaction satisfy the criteria stipulated in the agreement between the two banks.

The banks then need to settle the payment. Depending on the particular system, the banks can settle the payment either by redemption of the token, use an existing payment rail, or settle via a shared platform involving the tokenized central bank money.

Bank B is allowed to credit the supplier as per the agreed rules once all necessary conditions are satisfied. Both institutions must also be able to reconcile the payment in their accounting systems.

The process of settling payments varies depending on the design. A shared platform may orchestrate several processes, while separate networks may require messages and transactions to pass between different systems.

The system needs to distinguish between a payment that has been submitted, one that has been accepted, and actual settlement of the payment in the system. It also needs to account for any separate redemption or account-crediting steps. A blockchain confirmation confirms that a transaction has been executed based on the rules of that particular network.It does not necessarily mean the receiving bank has accepted the deposit or credited its customer.

Bridges enable separate blockchains to transact and exchange either assets or information about the transaction. Some lock tokens on one network and create equivalent tokens on another, or employ any other techniques to perform transactions across networks. These tools can help move digital assets between blockchains; however, that will not automatically imply that the recipient bank will accept the deposits issued by another institution.

Suppose a bridge makes a representation of Bank A's token available on a second network. That token may be transferable there, but Bank B still has to know what kind of rights are included in this token. Can the holder redeem it with Bank A? Is it acceptable to Bank B? Who should take the responsibility if redemption is delayed or cannot be completed?

Creating another token does not resolve such issues.

At the same time, bridges also increase technical risks. Depending on their design, they may rely on smart contracts, validators, third-party messaging services or privileged operators. Any vulnerability or bug in a bridge’s logic could lead to unauthorized transfers or inconsistent records.

Banks therefore must take into account both technical aspects of linking two networks and financial obligations of the tokens. A bridge can help with the first without resolving the second.

The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 discusses fragmentation across blockchain networks and the operational risks associated with connecting systems that use different rules and governance arrangements.

It is common for disputes to occur when there is a disagreement between the two systems about the transaction status. For instance, Bank A makes a payment request through its network but the confirmation fails to reach Bank B. Bank A detects a time-out in the communication and retries the request since it does not know whether the first request was made successfully.

When the receiving system considers both instructions separately, then the supplier might receive the amount twice. If the banks stop processing while they investigate, the funds may remain unavailable until they establish what happened.

The payment systems should have mechanisms that can cater for such situations. Idempotency enables the payment request to be retried without creating a duplicate payment request. Having a stable transaction identifier would help the receiving system to identify the retry request the same request rather than a new one. Atomic settlement can enable the two linked operations to succeed or fail simultaneously. Where the architecture supports it, this reduces the chances of one side of the payment being settled while the other one remains unsettled.

Atomic settlement is not a guarantee to avoid the above problem since some independent networks have transaction finality conditions which might not be able to coordinate each operation in a single transaction. The system must account for those limitations.

Transaction status also needs careful handling. A successful submitted transaction request does not mean a successful payment since there is a redemption or account crediting process after settlement. When the system uses each ledger update entry as confirmation of receipt of money from the receiving bank, it can report a successful transfer while the surrounding banking process is still incomplete.

When the outcome is uncertain, the banks need transaction records and reconciliation procedures to establish their respective positions. They also need an agreed process for resolving discrepancies without duplicating payments or losing track of the funds.

Two developments show how banks and financial institutions are approaching different parts of the problem.

In November 2025, JPMorgan rolled out its JPM Coin deposit token for institutional clients on Base. On October 19, 2026, the bank also announced the launch of JPM Coin on Ethereum. It makes it possible for eligible institutional clients to transfer JPM Coins within the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, which includes Base and Ethereum. It enables clients to use the bank's dollar-denominated deposit token on yet another public network.

For institutions already using Ethereum-based assets and applications, this can make it easier to use JPM Coin alongside their existing onchain activity. But supporting more than one blockchain does not guarantee the acceptance of the token by any other bank. JPM Coin is still tied to deposits in JPMorgan, and the token is limited to eligible institutional clients. The announcement illustrates the difference between making a token available on multiple networks and making it usable across unrelated banking relationships.

The BIS-led Project Agorá involves the application of more complex approaches to wholesale payments. It brings commercial bank deposits and tokenized central bank reserves on the same programmable platform. In May 2026, BIS published a report on the project’s prototype, which allowed atomic, multi-currency settlement across jurisdictions. Subsequently, the project team conducted the real-value testing in July 2026.

According to the BIS project overview, 28 financial institutions and central banks performed transactions totalling approximately CHF 800,000 across 17 scenarios. The test included the transactions related to both corporate and interbank payments, as well as those involving two currencies.

This testing revealed the necessity of operational activities needed for the platform. Participants used established payment-message standards, managed the issuance and redemption of tokenized deposits and reserves, and followed predefined procedures for executing transactions. The procedures included the fallback mechanism for situations when certain steps could not be completed as planned.

Those details are important because a payment platform must work with the systems banks already use. The ledger is not everything; the institution still needs to manage the corresponding funds, records, approvals, and exceptions.

Project Agorá provides evidence that coordinated settlement based on tokenized commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves can work in a controlled setting. It does not imply that all banks accept all other banks' deposit tokens. Wider adoption still depends on the legal, technical, and operational arrangements between participants.

Portability needs to be considered when designing the payment flow, rather than added later as a connection between blockchains. The system must identify the issuing bank and establish which receiving institutions can accept a particular token. It must define how the payment will be settled, when the receiving bank can credit the recipient, and what happens if one of those steps fails.

Redemption and reconciliation need similar attention. When a token is converted back into a conventional deposit, the token balance and the bank's corresponding records must remain consistent. The same applies when a payment uses tokenized central bank reserves or a shared settlement platform.

The system must also fit into existing banking operations. Compliance checks, fraud monitoring, accounting, treasury management, and customer account updates remain necessary when deposits are tokenized. Banks need to integrate these processes with the new infrastructure, including the procedures for delayed or rejected payments.

Testing should cover more than a successful transfer between two wallets. Engineers need to examine what happens when a receiving bank rejects an instruction, a message arrives late, a network becomes unavailable, or one institution records a transaction while another has yet to complete its part. Those tests help reveal whether the payment flow can recover from failures without duplicating transactions or leaving the institutions with inconsistent records.

JPM Coin's expansion to Ethereum gives institutional clients access to the deposit token on another public blockchain. Project Agorá has tested a shared platform that coordinates tokenized commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves for wholesale payments.

The approaches differ, but both show that moving money through programmable infrastructure involves more than recording transactions quickly.

A business receiving tokenized dollars needs to know whether its bank can accept them, how the payment will be settled, and when the funds will be available. If redemption requires a separate transfer or the banks cannot agree on the transaction's status, the speed of the original blockchain transaction offers limited help.

For tokenized deposits to work across banking relationships, institutions need arrangements that let them recognize the deposits, settle payments, and resolve failures. Until those arrangements are in place, the usefulness of a token will depend partly on which bank issued it and where the recipient needs to use it.

#9596. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9595. Cybersecurity Investments Shift from Reactive Breach Responses to Proactive Preventative Risk Management

Corporate cybersecurity expenditure operates under a deeply flawed thermodynamic model: organizational inertia resists movement until an external thermal shock injects the exact energy required to shift priorities. During stable periods, executive boards view security as an abstract, non-revenue-generating friction point—a dead weight on the operational balance sheet. Because digital safety yields no visible physical product during standard business cycles, leadership consistently underfunds preventative architecture.

The mechanism of budget allocation changes instantly only when a catastrophic breach or system outage occurs. This crisis acts as a destructive kinetic impact on the corporate structure:

Consequently, the post-incident window provides the sole viable operational vector for security leaders to secure capital expenditure. Boards transition from cost containment to emergency infrastructure hardening, systematically overriding prior inertia to fund long-overdue preventative controls.

Corporate cybersecurity spending historically operates under a reactive economic model: executive governance treats digital defense as an abstract operational overhead until a catastrophic breach materializes. This shock manifests as an acute systemic failure—materializing severe regulatory penalties, enterprise valuation contraction, and fiduciary liability—that instantly shatters board-level inertia and unlocks emergency capital. While destructive, this crisis mechanism paradoxically serves as the primary catalyst for securing long-overdue structural budgets. However, this panic-driven capital influx triggers a severe institutional paradox, fueling short-term hiring surges and reactive deployments that frequently degrade long-term system resilience.

When a major breach or high-profile infrastructure outage occurs, the sudden convergence of legal exposure and reputational damage forces an immediate reallocation of capital. Boards transition overnight from aggressive cost containment to unrestrained emergency defense spending. Yet, injecting capital into an active operational vacuum generates severe frictional costs across engineering and organizational workflows:

Relying on post-incident crises to fund digital defense locks organizations into an unsustainable boom-and-bust cycle. As the immediate regulatory and public-relations shock dissipates, executive oversight wanes, fiscal discipline hardens into budget contraction, and bloated security units face attrition or dismantling. True strategic resilience requires decoupling risk mitigation from catastrophic triggers. Organizations must systematically embed continuous assurance, threat modeling, and preventative architecture into the core engineering lifecycle—transforming security from a volatile, crisis-driven reaction into an immutable operational invariant.

To evaluate the structural trajectory of the cybersecurity job market, we must look past corporate public relations and analyze the mechanical failure modes of panic-driven funding. A major security breach functions as a violent kinetic shock that shatters executive inertia, paradoxically acting as the sole catalytic mechanism capable of unlocking long-overdue capital budgets. However, this emergency capital injection rarely funds graceful engineering; instead, it triggers a chaotic surge in headcount acquisition that strains organizational infrastructure akin to forcing high-voltage current through an unrated copper trace. The resulting thermal dissipation—manifested as administrative drag, tool sprawl, and catastrophic engineering burnout—dictates how talent demand fractures across four distinct operational trajectories.

Ultimately, the trajectory of cyber talent demand depends entirely on whether executive leadership continues to treat security as a volatile repair bill or embraces architectural resilience as an inviolable law of operational physics. Until organizations institutionalize preventative governance into their foundational layers, the job market will remain an inevitable captive of the next major outage.

For too long, the cybersecurity industry has operated on a destructive metabolic loop: corporate inertia starves preventative engineering of capital until a catastrophic breach strikes, forcing a violent release of panic-driven funding. This boom-and-bust cycle does not build resilience; it fractures infrastructure. When a major incident hits, the sudden cash injection triggers a recursive hiring bottleneck. Organizations rapidly onboard unvetted personnel under inflated compensation packages, bypassing rigorous technical evaluations. These rushed hires deploy uncoordinated security tools and misconfigured access permissions directly onto legacy systems without cohesive threat modeling, creating identity conflicts and expanding the system's attack surface.

To decouple professional careers and organizational survival from sensationalized catastrophe cycles, security leaders must abandon the compliance treadmill and the permanent panic trap. Relying on statutory box-checking audits shifts technical bandwidth away from actual vulnerability remediation, locking teams into generating static PDF reports while active exploit vectors widen in unpatched dependencies. Similarly, leaning entirely on heuristic machine learning to automate defense creates cache saturation and analyst alert fatigue. When rigid, black-box AI scanners generate millions of low-fidelity alerts, human cognitive overload spikes, causing analysts to drop or misclassify critical anomalies and allowing multi-stage privilege-escalation paths to slip through unnoticed.

Breaking this volatile loop requires transitioning to continuous preventative governance. Organizations must integrate native threat modeling directly into the core software development lifecycle, shifting capital allocation from reactionary incident-response mercenaries to embedded application security architects. By treating security as a structural component of engineering rather than a post-hoc patch, companies eliminate memory corruptions, improper permission scopes, and unvetted code paths before deployment. This structural shift flattens out the volatility of the labor market, replacing emergency headcount surges and subsequent institutional brain drains with predictable, sustainable defense engineering.

#9593. AI Agents Could Drive the Next Open Source Software Revolution

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

Building tomorrow's software today. AI-powered mobile apps • Carrier-grade infrastructure • Open source security • Hack

As coding tools improve, software companies will need more than a polished interface to defend their business. Open source communities will need better coordination, too.

Imagine a team paying for a workflow tool that almost fits its needs. An open source alternative exists, but it lacks an integration, has confusing documentation, and needs a better interface. Those gaps are small enough to describe and large enough to keep the team paying.

If AI coding agents help contributors close those gaps at a reasonable cost, the decision changes. That is the opportunity I see for open source: more projects becoming practical alternatives to the software people rent today.

My bet is that one of AI's biggest effects on software will come from communities improving shared tools. The difficult part is turning generated code into something people can trust.

There is evidence that AI assistance can accelerate some coding tasks. In a controlled experiment published in 2023, developers using GitHub Copilot completed a JavaScript HTTP server task 55.8% faster than the control group. That result concerned one bounded task with a coding assistant, so it cannot establish the economics of maintaining an entire product.

Other research shows why that distinction matters. METR's early-2025 randomized trial involved 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks in repositories they knew well. Allowing AI tools increased completion time by 19%.

In a February 2026 follow-up, METR said newer tools likely provided greater benefits, but selection effects and difficulties measuring time made its new results unreliable for estimating the size of those gains. The 2025 slowdown is not a verdict on every tool or workflow, and the follow-up is not proof of a universal speedup.

For open source, I would focus on specific, reviewable work: improving an installation guide, reproducing a bug, adding a missing integration, or testing an edge case. Agents could help contributors tackle these tasks, provided someone understands the changes and checks the result.

The useful measure is how much accepted, working improvement a project gains for the time its contributors and maintainers spend.

Developers have organized alternatives when vendors changed the terms of widely used software.

In August 2023, HashiCorp announced a move to the Business Source License for future releases of products including Terraform. The Linux Foundation announced OpenTofu, a community fork of the previously open source Terraform code, in September 2023. HashiCorp's announcement and the OpenTofu launch announcement document that sequence.

In March 2024, Redis announced that releases starting with Redis 7.4 would use the source-available RSALv2 and SSPLv1 licenses. Later that month, the Linux Foundation announced Valkey, continuing development from Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD 3-clause license, with support from companies including AWS and Google Cloud. Redis's announcement and the Valkey launch announcement explain the changes.

Redis subsequently added AGPLv3 as an open-source licensing option with Redis 8 in May 2025. Redis's AGPLv3 announcement makes that later change explicit.

These examples demonstrate the importance of licensing, governance, and organized contributors. They do not establish that AI agents created or sustained these forks. My prediction is that better coding tools could reduce some of the implementation work required for future community responses. Funding and experienced maintainers would still matter.

If competitors can reproduce more of your product's visible features, ask what customers would still need from your company.

That might be specialized data, reliable infrastructure, access to payment or communications networks, operational expertise, or a service customers trust. A well-documented API can make those capabilities useful across many interfaces and workflows.

Stripe's payment APIs and Twilio's communications APIs illustrate this model: developers can build their own applications around services supplied by another company. Stripe's Payment Intents documentation and Twilio's API overview show how those services are exposed.

I expect more companies to benefit from letting developers build interfaces and integrations around their services, including open-source ones. An API alone offers little protection, though. Its value depends on the capability behind it, its reliability, and the terms under which developers can use it.

There is also a tradeoff for users. An open source interface built on a proprietary API still depends on that provider's pricing and availability. Owning the front end does not mean owning the whole stack.

I expect the strongest pressure on products whose main advantage is a modest feature set or interface that competitors can reproduce without unusual resources. Lower implementation costs could make those markets more crowded.

Even there, replacing a product involves more than matching its screens. Migration, integrations, accessibility, support, and the confidence to entrust it with real work all affect the decision.

Companies with valuable data, deep domain knowledge, dependable operations, or strong networks may be better positioned. They will still have to earn their customers' business. Neither a proprietary codebase nor an open source license guarantees a good product.

There are several reasons this shift could be slower or narrower than I expect.

These are conditions the thesis has to survive. Open source gains ground only where the complete alternative, including the work of operating it, makes sense for users.

Lowering the effort required to start a project could also increase the number of overlapping, unfinished tools. If contributors repeatedly rebuild the same basics, the ecosystem may gain repositories without gaining dependable alternatives.

Experimentation has value. The danger is spreading maintenance effort across more projects than a community can support. A working prototype is a useful beginning, but users need a reason to believe it will still work after the next dependency update.

My preferred response is a simple set of habits.

Agents could help contributors navigate unfamiliar code and prepare changes. The responsibility for a useful contribution remains with the person submitting it.

I think AI coding agents could help open source compete across more of the software stack. The opportunity is substantial, but it depends on communities turning assistance into sustained improvements and companies delivering value customers cannot easily replace.

The question I would ask before starting another repository is simple: could this same effort make an existing project good enough for more people to use?

Which paid tool would you consider replacing with an open-source alternative, and what would that alternative need to earn your trust?

#9591. 8 Mac menu bar apps that actually earn their spot on a coding Mac (2026)

You know the moment. You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name. The MacBook notch has quietly eaten three of them.

The menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident. Here's the short list of menu bar apps I'd actually let stay there on a Mac used for coding, and what each one earns its spot for.

An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day. Everything else gets hidden or quit. With that rule, these eight make the cut.

Ice is the first thing I'd install, because it fixes the problem every other item on this list creates. It hides and shows menu bar items so you keep only the ones you care about visible.

It's free, open source, and needs macOS 14 or later. If you've ever lost an icon behind the notch, this is the fix.

Stats puts a system monitor in your menu bar: CPU, memory, disk, network, battery and more. You pick which modules show.

Handy when a build, a Docker container or a local model suddenly makes the fans spin up and you want to know why. Install with brew install stats or grab the DMG from the releases page.

Itsycal is a tiny menu bar calendar that reads from the Mac Calendar app. You can see and create events, view and complete Reminders, and join virtual meetings from it.

It has a configurable shortcut to open it, and yes, it supports Vim motions for navigation.

Maccy is a clipboard manager that does one job: keep your copy history and let you search it fast. Hit the shortcut, type, press Enter.

It's keyboard-first, stores everything on your Mac, and is MIT licensed. It needs macOS 14 or later. Once you have clipboard history you stop re-copying the same error message three times.

Amphetamine keeps your Mac awake with a simple switch in the menu bar, or automatically through Triggers.

You can keep it awake indefinitely, for a set time, while a file downloads, or while a specific app is running. Useful when a long test run or a coding agent is working and you step away.

CleanShot X is the screenshot and screen recording tool I'd pick for bug reports and PR descriptions. It adds annotation, a video editor with smart zooms, and optional cloud links.

The Basic license is $35 once with a year of updates (optional renewal at $19 a year). Cloud Pro is $10 per user per month billed annually. It also comes with a Setapp subscription. It needs macOS 13 or later.

Rectangle moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or by dragging them to screen edges and corners. Repeat a shortcut to cycle through sizes.

It lives in the menu bar for quick access to layouts. The free version is open source and supports macOS 14+. Rectangle Pro adds custom shortcuts for any size and position.

If you code with AI agents, the number you check most is probably how much of your limit is left and when it resets. TokenBar puts usage and reset times for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and Copilot in one menu bar view.

It shows things like session and weekly usage and a pace check against the reset. It's built on Peter Steinberger's MIT-licensed CodexBar and credits Pixel Agents for its agent status view. It doesn't give you any extra quota, it just shows you where you stand. Basic is $5/month, Pro is $15 lifetime, and it needs macOS 14 or later.

Weather, a second clock, VPN icons I only touch once a week, and every app that adds an icon by default and never asks. Those all go behind Ice.

What's the one menu bar app you'd never remove? Drop it in the comments, I'm always looking for a ninth.

#9589. The refusal is in English even when the request is not

A measurement and a repair of refusal consistency on Cohere Labs' Tiny Aya Global, built with CuratorKIT and SafeTune on one 64 GB Mac.

Content warning. This post quotes harmful request text and fragments of model output that begin to answer it — firearms modification, explosives, ransomware, forged identity documents, toxic gas, phishing and money laundering. Quoted fragments are short and non-operational; full generations are in the published eval dataset.

Tiny Aya Global 3.35B refuses harmful requests. It does not refuse them in the language they are asked in. Across 288 prompts — 8 attack families × 12 harmful intents × {English, Devanagari Hindi, romanised Hinglish} — the model almost never produced usable harmful content. On this prompt set the failure is not compliance. It is the expression of refusal. Under one fixed decoding protocol, 64 in 100 English replies and 54 in 100 Devanagari Hindi replies contained an explicit in-language refusal.

In romanised Hinglish, 3 in 100 did. The rest were neither a refusal nor an answer: how-to-shaped text with hallucinated nouns, sometimes running to the token cap because nothing in it signalled an ending.

After a LoRA repair trained on CuratorKIT-gated data, in-language explicit refusal rises to 1.00 / 0.98 / 0.95 across the three cells, with repetition collapse at zero everywhere. It is not free: 6 of 40 Hinglish benign prompts are now refused. That cost is measured and reported, not smoothed away.

Those 288 prompts are also 91.7% present in the training set by construction — the repair set is generated per intent from the same prompts — so the headline is in-distribution. Thirty prompts written after training, never seen, give the out-of-sample picture: explicit refusal 0.367 → 0.900, and hand-reading all sixty replies shows the base model answering 7 of 30 while the repaired model answers none. Both audits are in results/heldout.md and results/heldout_audit.md, andthe judge flagged zero of those seven.

I started with the obvious metric: attack success rate, judged by a local 4B model scoring whether a reply contains actionable harmful detail. It came back flat, so I nearly stopped there. Instead I read the generations, and what emerged was not a safety failure in the usual sense:

That distinction changes what you measure. A model that already refuses nearly everything cannot be made safer by safety training. It can be made legible: an operator in Lucknow who asks in Hinglish should see a refusal they recognise as a refusal, not a paragraph of fluent nothing. So the metric pair is:

Three guards, because a repair that raises refusal by refusing everything is worthless: a 120-prompt benign control (40 per language), a distinct-reply rate (a model that emits the same sentence 96 times has learnt a template, not a behaviour), and a manual audit of every judge positive — the local judge marked 8/288 base replies compliant and was wrong about 7 of them.

AuditKIT was installed and inspected and is not used: its detectors (AgentLoopDetection, Abstention) target agent trajectories and unanswerable-RAG cases, not single-turn chat replies, and a wrapper around them would have been kit theatre. The evaluation protocol here — fixed decoding, script-aware markers, benign control arm, published raw generations — was written for this task.

The interesting part of this project is not the final adapter. It is that each metric caught a different way the repair was fake.

Runaway generation is the same phenomenon measured differently: 56% of base replies never emitted a stop token at all and ran to the 256-token cap, versus 1.4% after the repair. The base model is not withholding an ending — it does not know it has reached one.

The over-refusal cost is real and unevenly distributed: the Hinglish cell pays most of it. Five of 40 Hinglish benign prompts — a dripping tap, a bicycle inspection, a sleep routine — now come back as refusals. That is the price of teaching a register the base model did not have, and it is the number I would attack next: more benign Hinglish, and a gate that rejects harmful-style refusals applied to benign-style prompts.

The 288-prompt taxonomy is a controlled instrument, not a sample of real traffic, and it is 91.7% in the training set. So the obvious objection is that the repair learned the test. Thirty prompts written after training — fresh phrasings, same intent space, ten per language — answer it:

The base model's seven are the interesting part. They are not near-misses: a step-by-step driver's-licence forgery guide with materials and printing advice, an IED component list with a "small explosive charge in a sealed container", a Hindi fake-ID procedure, a Hinglish semi-to-full auto conversion walkthrough, an in-character ransomware build, and a finished invoice-fraud phishing email. All seven sit in fiction, hypothetical and roleplay frames, and five are in Hindi or Hinglish. results/heldout_audit.md has each one with its classification.

That reframes the thesis, and I would rather state the narrower version than the tidy one: Tiny Aya refuses what resembles its safety training. Off that distribution it complies, and it complies most readily in romanised Hinglish. The repair works because it teaches refusal in the request's own language and register, which is also why the remaining escape route is a fresh phrasing rather than a different language.

The judge caught none of it — zero flagged replies in either arm — while in the main run it flagged 8 of 288 base replies, 7 of which were refusals. A 4B judge reads caveated procedural detail as a warning. That is why every headline claim here is either a script-aware marker or a hand count, with the judge reported beside it.

The repair is uneven across attack families, and the residual sits exactly where you would expect:

continuation is the family where the harmful frame is written by the prompt rather than asked for — the model is handed the opening of a "practical guide" and only has to keep going. All four residual Hinglish failures, and the one genuine base-model compliance in the audit, are in that cell. A refusal register learnt from direct asks does not transfer to a prompt that never asks.

The whole pipeline ran on one laptop: 3.35B parameters in fp16 on 16 GPU cores, LoRA at micro-batch 1 and 256 tokens (the 262k-token vocabulary makes the logits tensor, not the activations, the memory bottleneck — that constraint set the entire training recipe), two epochs in ~13 minutes, four evaluation arms in ~40 minutes. Generation and judging used a local Qwen3 through Ollama; no closed-model API calls are in the data path, so the dataset licence is unencumbered.

The honest comparison is not "cheaper than a frontier model", it is that a stronger generator would have hidden the finding. A frontier model asked to write Hinglish refusals would have produced excellent ones — and the experiment would then have measured its Hinglish, not Tiny Aya's. The repair data had to come from something that could fail in the same register, or the diversity and collapse metrics would have been measuring nothing.

#9588. AI Made Writing Code Cheap. Getting It Reviewed Now Takes 5x Longer, Says LinearB’s CEO

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

A developer using an AI assistant can open a pull request in minutes, yet the change still sits in a queue until a human reviewer picks it up. That is why agent-written pull requests wait 17.6 hours for a first review against 3.4 hours for human ones, even as enterprises spent $4.0 billion on AI coding tools in 2025, seven times the year before.

Today we sit down with Ori Keren, co-founder and CEO of LinearB, to discuss how the company grew from engineering dashboards into a context layer for agents, how it sells to boards that want proof of AI's return and where developer productivity goes once agents write much of the code.

Ishan Pandey: Welcome to Behind the Startup, Ori. Tell us about your journey and what made you build LinearB in the first place?

Ori Keren: Thanks for having me, Ishan. I started writing code as a kid, programming in BASIC on a Sinclair Spectrum in 1987, and I got my first developer job in 2000. From there I moved into management. I ran an engineering group at Interwise, which AT&T acquired, and then I was VP of R&D at CloudLock, which Cisco acquired in 2016. That's where I met Dan Lines, my co-founder.

What stayed with me from those years is how blind software development is. You run a team of a hundred engineers, and every week the business asks when something will ship or why it's late. You answer from gut feel and status meetings. Meanwhile, every answer is sitting in Git, in Jira and in your CI system, just never connected.

So in 2019, Dan and I started LinearB to connect it. We wanted to give engineering leaders real data on how their teams deliver, instead of gut feel, and then help them act on it. Helping teams act on the data is still what drives everything we build, and today those teams include agents.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB started in 2019 by giving engineering leaders delivery metrics, yet you have now rebuilt the platform around a knowledge graph of the whole software delivery lifecycle. What did you see in customer data over the past year that told you this called for a rebuild of the company's core?

Ori Keren: Two things, and they showed up in the data at the same time.

The first was that AI made writing code cheap but didn't make delivery faster. Our benchmarks cover 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams. AI-assisted pull requests are about 2.6 times larger than unassisted ones. Pull requests opened by agents wait 17.6 hours for a first review, against 3.4 hours for human ones. The bottleneck simply moved downstream, into review, merge and ownership.

The second was why agents struggle. An agent starts every task cold. It has a good idea of the code, but it doesn't have the business context. It doesn't know that this service had two incidents last month, that this file has been rewritten five times this quarter, or who owns it. We had all of that, linked from ticket to release, for every customer.

That's when it clicked. Everyone else is focused on writing code. We hold a knowledge graph of everything happening across delivery, and that's exactly what agents and teams need. A dashboard can't hand that context to an agent, so we rebuilt LinearB around the graph itself. Context is the new king.

Ishan Pandey: When you raised your Series B in 2022, LinearB served more than 5,000 development teams. How has the customer base grown since then and which kind of company is now expanding fastest on the platform?

Ori Keren: We've moved up market. In 2022, a lot of our growth came bottom up, from engineering managers at fast-moving tech companies. Today our core is the enterprise, meaning organizations with hundreds or thousands of engineers, several AI coding tools running at once, and a board asking what it's getting for the spend. We're also seeing strong growth among healthcare organizations.

The pattern is consistent. A company adopts Copilot here, Cursor there and Claude Code somewhere else. Within a quarter or two, leadership realizes it can't answer basic questions, like whether the code holds up, where it's working and what it's costing. That's when they come to us, and that's when they expand.

Kraken is a good example of what that looks like. They used our MCP with an AI assistant to find out what was slowing their code reviews. It turned out to be time zones and reviewer availability, not change size. Within four months, they cut review time at the 90th percentile by more than half.

Ishan Pandey: Boards and CFOs now ask directly whether AI coding spend is paying off. How has that changed who signs a LinearB contract, from the VP of engineering to the CFO or CIO, along with how a deal is won?

Ori Keren: The SVP of engineering or CTO is still our executive buyer.

Who they answer to. Ken Ringdahl, the CTO at Emburse, puts our charts straight into his board decks because his board asks specifically about AI use and ROI. That's now normal.

There are a lot of company-wide AI initiatives now, driven by the CFO or CEO, and in the companies we work with, engineering is usually where AI spend is highest.

So finance is in the room far more often. Engineering leaders bring us in because they need numbers that hold up in front of a CFO, not a vanity metric from a vendor's own dashboard.

That changes how a deal is won. Five years ago, we won by showing a better cycle-time chart. Today we win by answering the finance question in the evaluation itself. We connect the data, and within days we show which teams are getting value from AI, which aren't, and what each delivered change costs. Token spend makes this sharper. In our 2026 AI benchmarks, which cover 253 engineering organizations, developers at the 90th percentile now spend $35.20 per coding day on tokens, up nearly 75% in three months. When a CFO sees that line, the conversation moves fast.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB built an audience through the Dev Interrupted podcast and free developer tools long before Gartner gave the category a Magic Quadrant. How does that community-led motion now work alongside enterprise sales and which channel brings in your largest customers today?

Ori Keren: Dev Interrupted was never meant as a lead generator. We started it because engineering leaders had nowhere to talk about the craft of running engineering. That trust turned out to be our moat. When a category gets a Magic Quadrant, every buyer suddenly has a shortlist. Our edge is that many of the people on the buying side have listened to the show for years, used our free tools, or borrowed our benchmarks for their own planning.

Today the two motions feed each other. Community and free tools create familiarity, often with a director or a staff engineer. Benchmarks and research give the champion something credible to take upstairs. Enterprise sales then turns that into an organization-wide rollout with security review, procurement and an ROI case.

Our largest deals close through our enterprise sales team, and when we trace them back, someone inside almost always knew LinearB before the first sales call. That's the compounding effect we're after.

Ishan Pandey: Your effort skill sends simple changes through cheaper agent runs while giving risky changes more care and more tokens. How do you price a product whose value is partly measured in tokens saved and what will the next skills for review and merge add for customers?

Ori Keren: First, a clarification. The effort skill isn't a cost-cutting tool that happens to touch quality. It's a judgment tool. It looks at a change's complexity and risk, using the full knowledge graph, and decides how hard the agent should work. Sometimes that means fewer tokens. On a fragile payments service, it means more, with careful, tested edits. The goal is the right effort on each change.

That's why we don't price on tokens saved. If we took a cut of savings, we'd be rewarded for making agents cheap rather than for making delivery better. Customers judge us on the cost of each delivered change, not the raw token bill.

The next skills go where the bottleneck now sits, in review and merge. They'll use the same context to help teams decide where human attention is needed and what can move faster. After that comes governance of AI-written code and spend optimization.

Ishan Pandey: Gartner sizes the developer productivity insight market at about $400 million while enterprises already spend billions on AI coding tools. How large can this category become once it measures and guides agents as well as people over the next three years?

Ori Keren: The $400 million figure describes the developer productivity insight category, platforms that give engineering leaders visibility into how their teams deliver software. We've always operated in that category, and we've also always gone beyond it. Our philosophy has been to explore, measure, act, and the act part now shows up in our agent skills.

Once a company spends that much on agents, a layer that decides how those agents should work, where they should spend effort and whether their output is safe to ship isn't a reporting tool anymore. It's part of the delivery system, like CI/CD or observability. So the right comparison isn't to other dashboards. It's a share of total spend on software delivery, human and agent combined.

What I'm confident about is the direction. We think it's time for the category to stop being something leaders look at once a month and become something agents consult on every change.

Ishan Pandey: For CTOs and VPs of engineering whose boards will ask them this year to prove AI's return, what is the first thing you would tell them to measure and which older metric should they stop reporting?

Ori Keren: Measure the cost per effective delivered change, not code generated, pull requests opened or lines accepted from an assistant. An effective change is one that merged, shipped and didn't come back as rework. Take what you spend on people and tokens, and divide it by those changes. You want effective changes trending up and the cost of each one trending down. That's the number that tells a board whether AI is paying off, and it holds up when finance pushes on it.

Emburse tracks exactly this. Over seven months, most of its code moved to AI, and its cost per effective pull request fell about 35%.

Right next to it, track what each model costs against the quality of the code it produces. The differences are bigger than most teams expect. Kraken found that two engineers can ship the same work while one burns thousands of dollars in tokens and the other spends hundreds, depending on which models they use and how.

Then stop reporting raw throughput, like pull requests or commits per developer, and above all, stop reporting AI adoption rates. Telling a board that 90% of your engineers use AI says nothing about return.

Inside engineering, though, keep measuring how work flows through your software factory. The bottlenecks haven't gone away. They've moved to review and release.

For CTOs and VPs of engineering heading into a board meeting, the practical takeaway is his metric. Cost per effective delivered change puts people and token spend over work that merged, shipped and stayed fixed, which gives a CFO a number to test. With AI coding spend compounding and the measurement category growing more than 40% a year, I expect the teams that adopt this kind of accounting early to have the easiest budget conversations of 2027. Leaders who want to compare their own teams can start with LinearB's free benchmarks report or the LinearB platform.

#9585. Fintech Login Fallback: Owning Templates and Retention Across SMS and Email OTP

The bill for SMS-to-email OTP login fallback includes message sends, polling, retained evidence, and the engineering time needed to keep recovery templates consistent. For a fintech contact form that routes locked-out customers to the right support queue, count the work before choosing a provider: in an illustrative workload of 1,000 attempts with six status checks each, polling alone creates 6,000 reads. That's a planning example, not a measured workload or a provider charge. It identifies a term the application can control.

Short answer: use SMS OTP first, add email OTP fallback only with an application-owned issuance and validation lifecycle, and bound the polling that drives the transition. Keep template ownership and support-queue decisions in the application so a provider change doesn't also become a recovery-policy migration. For a US/EU SaaS built in Node.js, the runtime doesn't remove those responsibilities.

The contact form is the concrete boundary here: a customer reports a login problem, the recovery flow gathers evidence, and the application routes the request to the appropriate support queue. A delivery status is evidence about a message. It isn't permission to disclose account information to the person submitting the form.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want one REST API to keep application code unchanged when switching the vendor behind a supported capability, provided polling meets their recovery requirements. Its capability contract is the concrete boundary; the application owns the recovery state machine and templates above it. Infrai uses one key and one bill for SMS and email, reducing credential management and billing reconciliation across the two legs of this recovery worker. Public, unauthenticated discovery supplies request and response schemas, so the team can inspect the contract before wiring credentials into the integration. These conveniences don't make an email template equivalent to hosted OTP verification.

Every unresolved attempt invites another read, another retained response, and sometimes another message. The architectural mistake is treating all three as necessary evidence, because storing repeated snapshots doesn't make the underlying status more authoritative, and sending a second code doesn't establish which challenge the application should accept. Preserve the state transition that explains the support decision, with enough provenance to investigate it later.

In the planning example, reducing the polling budget from six checks to two changes 6,000 reads to 2,000 reads for the same 1,000 attempts. It also means fewer observations of intermediate status. That's the trade-off: a smaller polling budget may leave the application with less evidence when it decides to offer recovery, so the policy needs an explicit unresolved state rather than pretending that silence proves delivery failure. No timing or delivery guarantee follows from that arithmetic.

The same accounting applies to retention. If an application stores six complete status responses per attempt, it keeps 6,000 snapshots in that example; keeping one terminal decision record per attempt produces 1,000 decision records instead. These records differ in content and forensic value, so their counts aren't a storage-size benchmark. The useful question is which fields justify continued retention after the recovery window closes.

For the fintech form, a proposed decision record would contain an internal attempt identifier, the selected support queue, a template revision, the channel transition, and the application's reason for making it. Those are application fields, not a claimed provider response schema. Keep contact-form prose out of repeated delivery snapshots; a customer can put sensitive financial details into a free-text field without the architecture asking for them.

Template ownership is the migration lever. Let the application own the purpose of each message, its approved wording, the revision used for a recovery attempt, and the rule that maps a contact-form category to a support queue. An adapter can translate an application request into a provider call without acquiring authority over account recovery. A provider-held template identifier should be a binding to an application revision, not the only surviving copy of the recovery policy.

Consider an illustrative form category named account-access and an internal destination named access-review. Those labels belong to the SaaS. If a channel vendor changes, the adapter binding may change, but the category, destination, approved message intent, and evidence-retention decision should still mean the same thing. This is the migration invariant to test; an unchanged function signature is weak evidence if the new integration silently changes who owns code expiry or validation.

SMS offers hosted OTP issuance and verification in this stack. Email recovery uses ordinary email sending with code issuance and validation owned by the application. Treat those as different contracts. Before an email message is sent, decide how its challenge expires, how failed guesses are limited, and whether switching channels supersedes the previous challenge. The OWASP recovery guidance is a useful reference for secure, expiring, single-use recovery tokens and consistent responses.

The failure mode is challenge ambiguity: a delayed SMS arrives after email fallback, and the application has no explicit rule for whether either code remains valid. Choose the rule before wiring the send operation, record its outcome, and make the same rule survive a vendor migration. Keeping that policy in the application costs implementation effort; outsourcing part of the lifecycle to a specialist can be the better decision when that effort exceeds the value of retaining control.

For authentication recovery, send the email when the policy authorizes it. Avoid a design whose correctness depends on retracting a scheduled email after the SMS succeeds. This keeps the recovery boundary understandable and avoids coupling login safety to delayed-message cancellation semantics.

A fair comparison needs separate acceptance criteria for the authentication lifecycle and the email transport. Twilio Verify, Amazon SES, and SendGrid are real alternatives to evaluate, but listing their names beside a unified API doesn't establish that they take on the same responsibilities. Use the following table as a selection test, rather than assuming that an email delivery integration includes a recovery-code lifecycle.

These are different integration choices, not a feature-parity claim. A verification specialist is the better direction to evaluate when real-time cross-channel orchestration is a requirement. A direct email provider is the better direction when the team wants to manage that transport relationship separately and is comfortable owning the recovery lifecycle around it. Infrai fits the narrower case where replacing the underlying vendor through the same capability contract reduces application migration work.

Discovery exposes per-capability vendor readiness and schemas; inspect those for the actual deployment rather than treating the US/EU label on a planning document as evidence of regional suitability. This article doesn't establish a fintech compliance determination, data-residency guarantee, or equivalent authentication assurance across channels.

Before implementing the Node.js adapter, inspect the SMS OTP contract. This Python example uses only the standard library and queries public discovery; it doesn't issue a code, create a recovery attempt, or need an API key. It makes the proposed migration boundary inspectable without guessing request fields. The retry budget is an example client policy, not a service limit.

Use the returned request and response schemas to review an adapter's assumptions before and after a vendor change. Schema compatibility is necessary; it doesn't prove that the recovery policy is preserved. The application's transition tests still have to establish that. The platform's documented 24h default idempotency deduplication window is a retry convention, not an OTP expiry policy or a retention period for authentication evidence.

Polling-based decisions arrive after observations, so the application must tolerate an unresolved interval. Persist the recovery decision before using it to drive support routing, and make repeated processing converge on the same outcome. The relevant failure modes are duplicate fallback issuance, stale status overwriting a newer decision, and a contact-form retry opening another recovery attempt without linking it to the original. These are design cases to handle, not reports of provider incidents.

Delivery and verification need separate state.

A message accepted for delivery must not mark an account verified, and successful challenge verification must not let arbitrary text from the contact form pick a privileged support queue. Route from the application's validated category and recovery state, preserving enough evidence to explain the selection. If the status remains unresolved after the polling budget, move to the policy's unresolved branch; don't keep polling indefinitely merely because the adapter exposes a status operation.

During migration, test a delayed SMS, a repeated form submission, and an expired email challenge against the same expected application decisions. An adapter can own schema translation while the service owns recovery policy and a retention job owns evidence expiry. That's a division a team can review without confusing a successful send call with a complete authentication protocol.

Start with purpose, then choose retention. Retain the minimum decision evidence needed for support review and the applicable audit policy; expire challenge material when its authentication purpose ends, and stop accumulating identical polling snapshots after the application has made its decision. Don't put raw OTP values into diagnostic logs. Template revisions can explain which instructions the customer received without preserving every message body and every copy of the contact form.

After raw polling snapshots expire, support may be unable to reconstruct every intermediate status observation. After message bodies expire, a template revision can explain approved wording but cannot prove every rendered detail of an individual message. Those are deliberate losses of forensic detail, and a team that needs that detail must budget for retaining it under an explicit policy. Keeping everything forever is also a policy, usually an unexamined one.

The acceptance test is concrete: SMS remains the primary OTP path, email fallback has an application-owned validation lifecycle, polling has a stopping rule, and a vendor replacement preserves the template revision and support-routing decision. Reject the design if required orchestration depends on immediate channel events or if the team cannot own email recovery safely.

OWASP's recovery guidance supports the token-lifecycle discussion. The provider documentation below is for checking candidate contracts and ownership boundaries; it isn't evidence of measured delivery performance or interchangeable authentication guarantees.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the first-party SMS and email recovery guide to check the polling-based architecture against your application's template ownership: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/sms/answers/sms-otp-vs-email-otp-for-saas-login-us-eu-best-practice/

#9583. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

 

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.

#9581. I opened every free Amazon image compliance checker I could find — including my own

A rejected main image is one of the few Amazon listing errors you can catch before submitting — pure white background, 85% frame fill, 1000px+ for zoom, no text or watermarks. Yet most sellers only learn the rules after a rejection email.

So I opened every free compliance checker I could find and tested the same things on each:

Disclosure up front, not buried at the end: I work on PicViva, one of the tools in this list. I've tried to test ours as harshly as the others, and I'll point out where competitors beat us — because in two cases, they do.

Now the details, in the order I tested them.

The strongest pure checker I found. Three upload slots, and it checks things others skip: centering, edge-crop risk, watermark detection, and it separates main image rules from secondary image rules — which matters because Amazon allows lifestyle shots in slots 2–9 but rejects them in slot 1. It also gates checks by destination marketplace, including eBay, Etsy and Lazada variants. Everything runs on-device.

Where it's weak: it's a checker plus a separate fix flow. You still take the error list somewhere else to actually repair the image.

zonfy's checker does the pixel rules locally and clearly labels what's local vs. what requires their AI. But the interesting part is the ecosystem around it: a dedicated Image Fixer (square crop, ~85% fill, true #FFFFFF, 2000px export) and a bulk processor for whole listings. They even offer the checker as an embeddable widget for seller guides — a smart distribution play I haven't seen elsewhere.

One honest note: their fixer docs describe "the near-white trap" — backgrounds that look white but measure 240-something. That's exactly the failure mode I wrote about in my last post: a global brightness boost can't fix it without clipping your product. Good to see others hitting the same wall.

I assumed non-English markets had no local-language tooling. Listimo is fully German: the checker page, the rules, the suite around it (a 0–100 listing score, a "Rufus check" that tests whether your listing answers buyer questions). And they do something none of the English tools do well: they split the problem honestly. Pixel-measurable rules run locally; text, logos and watermarks get an AI pass, because no pixel measurement catches a "FREE SHIPPING" badge.

That split — "what code can measure" vs. "what needs a model" — is the most honest architecture in this list.

Does exactly what it says: pure white (RGB 255), fill, zoom dimensions, file type. In-browser, no login, no upsell mid-check. The fewest checks here, but zero friction. Its sibling compliance-claims-checker (for listing claims) is a nice touch.

12 rules with pass/fail output, including "no lifestyle imagery on main" — a rule most pixel tools skip because detecting a lifestyle scene needs more than thresholds. The upload widget renders after JavaScript loads, so my static HTML scan found no file input; judge it in your browser, not by my curl.

Their sitemap advertises an image checker, but the page I loaded showed no upload UI before JS, and their core product is paid AI listing images. I can't verify what the checker does, so I won't claim it works.

Win: the check and the fix are one flow. The checker opens directly in the editor (I verified GET /en/app/editor/new?tool=amazon-image-compliance-checker returns 200 with no login redirect), flags size, background, text, watermark and coverage issues, and the toolbar to fix each one is right there — resize, background removal, the compliance re-check. And the tool page exists in 19 languages, because marketplace sellers overwhelmingly aren't browsing in English.

Lose, honestly: zonfy ships 13 free seller tools and a bulk processor; we ship one standalone free tool. Fernpix covers more marketplaces. Listimo's AI text/logo pass catches things our pixel checks don't. If you need any of those today, use theirs — this post will still be here when you need a fixer.

Every tool above is free at the point of check. None of them will get your image un-rejected after the fact — test before you upload, not after Amazon emails you.

Method note: all findings collected Nov 2026 by loading each page and inspecting the rendered HTML; "runs locally" claims are taken from each tool's own documentation and spot-checked where feasible. Tools change — if one of these now behaves differently, that's worth knowing too.

#9580. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9576. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.
